item.title: 26 mil reproducciones · 330 reacciones | Nos EUA - Um brasileiro de 46 anos foi preso no último domingo (4) após aparecer vestido como um agente do Serviço de Imigração e Controle de Alfândegas dos Estados Unidos (ICE, na sigla em inglês) em um local de votação das eleições brasileiras Miami, na Flórida. ➡️​ Segundo o gabinete do xerife do condado de Miami-Dade, Danilo Silva circulava pelo campus de Kendall do Miami Dade College, onde brasileiros votavam, usando boné e jaqueta com identificação do ICE, óculos escuros, máscara cobrindo o rosto e botas táticas. De acordo com o relatório policial, ele caminhava pelos locais de votação e abordava pessoas na intenção de causar medo entre os eleitores. A NBC filmou o momento da prisão. Após receber as denúncias, agentes uniformizados e investigadores à paisana passaram a monitorar a área. Em determinado momento, Silva foi confrontado por dois homens, um deles filmando a situação. Os envolvidos iniciaram uma discussão, e os investigadores intervieram. Questionado pelos policiais, Silva admitiu que não era agente federal. Segundo o relato, ele afirmou que as roupas eram uma "fantasia" comprada pela internet, na Amazon. Ainda de acordo com as autoridades, o homem disse que havia comparecido ao local para votar usando uma camisa da seleção brasileira. Depois, retornou ao carro, trocou de roupa e vestiu o uniforme semelhante ao utilizado por agentes do ICE. Aos investigadores, Silva afirmou que queria apenas "ver a reação das pessoas". ➡️​ Ele foi preso em flagrante. Segundo o relatório da polícia, durante a abordagem, ele ficou exaltado e ameaçou um dos investigadores, dizendo que ele se arrependeria da decisão de prendê-lo. Segundo o Miami Herald, em seguida, Silva tentou subornar os policiais para ser liberado. De acordo com o jornal, ele ofereceu dinheiro e disse que poderia mostrar a transferência pelo celular. Ele foi levado para o centro de detenção Turner Guilford Knight. Ele foi acusado de intimidação de eleitores, tentativa de suborno, uso ilegal de insígnias das forças de segurança e conduta desordeira. Saiba mais no #g1. #ice #brasileiro #estadosunidos #notícias #g1mundo | g1 - O Portal de Notícias da globo

item.title: They prob don’t have access to all the things that keep most humans sick- our foods, meds, drinks, caffeine…lack of exercise, laziness, additions. Thus reducing mental heath…
item.description: They prob don’t have access to all the things that keep most humans sick- our foods, meds, drinks, caffeine…lack of exercise, laziness, additions. Thus reducing mental heath issues that also cause physical harm to a person as well. Morgan Klar Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Global soil erosion outpaces natural recovery, report warns
item.description: Isaac Larsen, an associate professor in the College of Natural Sciences' Department of Earth, Geographic, and Climate Sciences, is a lead author of "Status of the World's Soil Resources 2026," a new report produced by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) that draws on recent scientific literature and contributions from hundreds of experts around the world. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Political orientation and institutional trust emerge as key factors in local wind energy support
item.description: Why does the expansion of wind energy sometimes meet with local resistance, even though renewable energy generally enjoys broad support? RIFS researcher Jörg Radtke used a representative survey of 6,284 people in North Rhine-Westphalia to investigate which social characteristics are linked to the acceptance of wind energy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Game simulator shows how math can guide decisions when resources are limited
item.description: In "Bloons Tower Defense," the goal is to stop balloons from reaching the end of a track by strategically placing towers along the route. These towers vary in cost, range and attack power, and they also take up valuable space. The game becomes increasingly difficult with each round. Where you place a tower therefore determines not only how effective it is now but also which options remain available later in the game. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Digital ibuprofen' offers Chinese youth comfort through cute characters facing familiar struggles
item.description: In China, young people are encountering a myriad of challenges, from societal pressures around success to life in a highly surveilled society, that have led them to turn to the internet in search of a balm to soothe their pain. What has emerged is a host of content called "digital ibuprofen"—viewed as a way to numb the anxieties of modern living. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Attention can't be bought, so brands turn to memes
item.description: The funniest post you saw this week may not have come from a friend; it may have come from a brand. Whether it is Kohl's, Wendy's, or Netflix, brands are behaving more like internet users than traditional advertisers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Unusual senses: The secret superpowers of amphibians and reptiles
item.description: The Surinam toad is one of the strangest frogs on Earth. Flat-bodied, tiny-eyed and adapted to the murky waters of the Amazon basin, it hunts well despite having very poor vision. When a fish swims close, the frog suddenly opens its mouth and sucks the prey inside in a fraction of a second. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Women in this Sardinian mountain village have high odds of living to 100. Researchers have identified it as a new blue zone—a geographic region where residents aged 70 ... Ver más

item.title: What a locust can teach us about how neuromodulators alter odor processing
item.description: When you walk into a bakery and smell fresh cookies, the enticing smell draws you in. After you eat a handful of cookies, though, the same smell likely doesn't send you back for more. Researchers in the McKelvey School of Engineering at Washington University in St. Louis sought to determine the biological mechanisms in the brain that controllably alters odor-evoked behavior by using an unlikely model—a locust. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rhinos and elephants can cause huge problems if reintroduced badly—here's how to get it right
item.description: Moving large animals around is a seductive idea in conservation. If there are plenty of animals in one place and too few in another, moving some between the two seems an obvious solution. Sometimes it is. But with animals as large, mobile and socially complicated as elephants and rhinos, the move itself can turn out to be the straightforward part. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Budding rocket scientists put designs to the test in outback competition
item.description: Domestic and international students turn a remote sheep station into a testing ground for their designs as they compete in the Australian Universities Rocket Competition. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Bill Ormonde and Sarah McConnell

item.title: D’Arros shearwater colony grew nearly 10-fold after rats were eradicated
item.description: D'Arros Island's Wedge-tailed Shearwater population rose dramatically after rats were eradicated in 2003. Researchers recorded 2,768 breeding pairs in 2016 and 2,406 pairs in 2021. The colony spread across a larger area and exhibited higher breeding burrow density during later surveys. The study utilized direct counts and area-based estimates to determine breeding pair numbers. Identifying the peak incubation period in November was crucial for future population comparisons. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Quantum interactions may have locked early universe's fields into existing energy states
item.description: The universe may be trapped in its own comfort zone, and a researcher in the College of Engineering and Computer Science has helped explain why it cannot seem to leave. A new study suggests the universe could be locked into its current state by the same kinds of quantum effects that scientists study when trying to preserve fragile information inside a quantum computer. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Does increased childcare funding help mothers into work?
item.description: Since Labor won the 2024 general election, policy focused on children in the early years—from birth to school age—and their parents has moved sharply up the political agenda. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Forests are dying along North Carolina's coast—and it's speeding up
item.description: A new study finds that coastal forest loss in North Carolina's Albemarle-Pamlico Peninsula began accelerating after 2010 and may still be speeding up. The study also found that North Carolina lost more than 20% of its coastal forest between 1985 and 2021. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: An iced coffee won't predict job performance—but it might reveal hiring bias
item.description: Imagine two candidates with identical qualifications interviewing for the same job. One arrives carrying a bottle of water, while the other walks in with an iced coffee. Should that difference matter? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Switching on brain cells: the Nobel-winning science of optogenetics
item.description: The Nobel medicine prize was awarded Monday to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their pioneering work in the neuroscience field of optogenetics. In optogenetics, scientists control neurones by stimulating them with light -- potentially unlocking breakthroughs for conditions such as dementia, depression and blindness. FRANCE 24's Monte Francis reports. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE24

item.title: NASA to Stream SpaceX Crew-12 Return, Splashdown Live
item.description: NASA and SpaceX are targeting no earlier than 8:05 a.m. EDT, Wednesday, Oct. 7, for the undocking of the agency’s SpaceX Crew-12 mission from the International Space Station, pending weather conditions. An Oct. 7 undock puts NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Taveau

item.title: Rare insect discovery reveals a new species from the dinosaur age
item.description: Some 99 million years ago, during the age of the dinosaurs, a tiny insect belonging to a species previously unknown to science became trapped in tree resin. The resin hardened and turned into amber, and the fossil preserved within it has now enabled a team of researchers from the School of Zoology and The Steinhardt Museum of Natural History to identify and describe a new species: Cretodorus noonoo, or "Noo-Noo." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How psychopathic traits shape language
item.description: Popular culture often depicts people with psychopathy as cold, emotionless and hollow, but a recent University of Mississippi study found that the language associated with psychopathic traits is more complicated than often described. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Experts deem empowering neurologists and neurology trainees to perform lumbar punctures at bedside a worthwhile goal
item.description: Many medical specialties now require graduating doctors to be skilled in point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) for diagnosing patients and performing procedures. POCUS uses a portable ultrasound device to help clinicians make fast, accurate medical decisions. The Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education lists this skill as an official milestone for graduation. Even though training is improving for its potential use in treating head, eye and nerve conditions, POCUS is only moderately used by neurologists dealing with some neurological conditions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient DNA evidence narrows down when people first reached the Americas
item.description: One of the unresolved mysteries about the history of the Americas is when the first people arrived. Despite extensive debate centering on genetic, archaeological and environmental evidence, there is still no consensus or conclusive proof. Did they enter before, during or after the coldest period of the last ice age, known as the Last Glacial Maximum? Evidence from recent analysis of ancient DNA is providing fresh clues. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Standard 3D printers let labs build and adapt tools for bacterial research
item.description: Studying microorganisms requires instruments with extremely high precision. Such instruments are expensive and take a long time to manufacture using traditional methods, which has slowed progress in the field. It has also been difficult for the biologists who use these instruments to participate directly in their development. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Astronomers catch a star slowly snacking on a brown dwarf, 300 light years away
item.description: Like Earth, most planetary bodies circle their star in stable, detached orbits. These companionable systems can suddenly change when a planet comes too close to its star. In such a close encounter, a star can pull the planet in and swallow it whole. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How game publishers set international prices: A study reveals four pricing approaches on Steam
item.description: Although digital platforms make it possible to sell the same product globally, prices often vary across countries because of differences in purchasing power, currencies, taxation and other market conditions. At the same time, the transparency of online prices enables consumers to compare prices across regions easily. Companies therefore must balance local affordability with the need to avoid excessive international price differences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A health app designed for teachers
item.description: A new app is designed to help teachers stay healthy in their day-to-day work. The digital tool is the result of a three-year collaborative project between the Technical University of Munich (TUM) and health insurance provider AOK Bayern. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Atomic motion could help push solar cells beyond conventional limits
item.description: The bulk photovoltaic effect (BPVE), a photoelectric effect that generates photocurrent without a p–n junction, can persist even when a material's average crystal structure remains centrosymmetric, a study from Institute of Science Tokyo has found. Researchers demonstrated this in CuCrP2S6, a van der Waals material that transitions from a noncentrosymmetric to a centrosymmetric average structure. The finding challenges the conventional view of BPVE and suggests a new strategy for enhancing photoelectric conversion. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: After losing her mother to MS, J.K. Rowling gave £10m to research
item.description: J.K. Rowling opened the Anne Rowling Regenerative Neurology Clinic in memory of her mother, who died of multiple sclerosis. The clinic focuses on research and treatment of various neurological diseases, including multiple sclerosis and Parkinson's disease. The funding aims to attract world-class researchers to develop new therapies and potentially find a cure. It has already hosted numerous clinical appointments and research projects since its inception. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Quantum systems never quite forget where they came from
item.description: Even the most chaotic quantum systems keep a permanent mark of their own past—a "quantum birthmark"—that never fades. Researchers from Tampere University, Harvard University and TU Dresden discovered the feature in their recent study. Their findings shed new light on the elusive relationship between classical and quantum mechanics. Looking ahead, these quantum birthmarks, along with related phenomena known as "scars," could eventually be harnessed to power next-generation nanoelectronics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Unmowed strips attract insects, but many abandon partially mowed dikes
item.description: Municipalities are increasingly mowing dikes and verges in stages, so that insects can make longer use of the plants growing there. Mowing is essential to keep a dike strong, explains ecologist Constant Swinkels of Radboud University. "If you don't mow, trees or sturdy shrubs such as blackberries may start to grow. You don't want that, because their roots are so thick that they can cause dikes to collapse." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A novel path to fusion ignition: Heat first, then add fuel
item.description: For more than 70 years, fusion energy researchers have used a particular equation to judge whether a plasma would stay hot and dense enough—for long enough—to reach a point where it could sustain itself without any more external power added. While that equation marks the finish line, also known as ignition, it says nothing about the best way to reach it. New research from the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL) maps a path to ignition conditions using far less energy than any other path. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sniffer dogs, bloodstain patterns and ballistics evidence under the microscope in new studies
item.description: CSI may have spawned innumerable spinoffs, but it turns out you can't trust TV—or sniffer dogs. New research is questioning the scientific basis for the dogs' use by police, as well as aspects of bloodstain pattern analysis and ballistics evidence routinely used in courts. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Florida Keys heat wave reveals nearly fourfold death risk for diseased coral
item.description: Disease and heat pose a deadly combination for coral reefs, according to a new University of Georgia study published in the journal Coral Reefs. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Russia is using Ukraine's children to win its occupation—and the wider war
item.description: A year or so after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the city of Murmansk in Russia's Arctic northwest marked its annual regional day with a celebration for children. Alongside the sons and daughters of Russian soldiers stood children taken from the occupied Prymorskyi district of Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Local tipping points in dune landscapes: How does a dune system organize itself?
item.description: Building with nature is an important concept in our coastal defense. After all, by harnessing natural processes, we are more resilient to sea level rise. A good understanding of these processes is therefore indispensable. Ecologist Paul Berghuis, affiliated with Utrecht University and the Royal Netherlands Institute for Sea Research (NIOZ), delved into the world of dune formation and discovered that within young dune landscapes, dunes and grasses do not arrange themselves randomly but follow a fixed pattern. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Detecting forever chemicals—with yeast and AI
item.description: If you're reading this, your body probably contains forever chemicals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists found at least 10 likely new species of bizarre branching worms inside sea sponges
item.description: Researchers have identified ten likely new species of branching marine worms found within sea sponges. These unusual worms exhibit a unique tree-like body structure, which has evolved over time. Genetic analysis and museum specimens helped resolve the long-standing classification issues of these marine organisms. The study indicates these worms' diversification relates closely to their sponge hosts and geographic locations. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: ESA at IAC 2026 – Day 1
item.description: Stronger European capabilities and deeper international cooperation were at the heart of ESA’s first day at the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) in Antalya, Türkiye. From exploration to the contribution of space to society, ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher underlined the importance of Europe becoming a stronger and more capable partner in a rapidly changing space environment. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: "Lo hice para vengar a Gaza, quería morir como mártir": el copiloto del vuelo de Flydubai confesó por qué atacó al piloto
item.description: Hammam Al-Hammami fue interrogado por los investigadores de Emiratos Árabes Unidos. Mientras, Israel busca determinar si el piloto actuó solo o si fue enviado por otra persona. Fuente: Clarín - Mundo.
item.dc:creator: Clarin.com - Home

item.title: Tracking uncovers $80 million spent on AI political ads, most without disclosure
item.description: The 2026 U.S. midterm campaigns are the first in which AI-generated political ads are regularly appearing on people's televisions and social media feeds. We are researchers who have been studying political advertising through the Wesleyan Media Project since 2010. This election cycle—using data from media reports, student coders and AdImpact, a firm that tracks political ad spending—we've tracked about $80 million in spending on almost 170 unique ads that use AI. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sharks' inner ears reveal surprising diversity that may reflect evolution more than environment
item.description: A new study of shark anatomy suggests the shape of their inner ears is far more variable than expected, and this variation could have more to do with their evolutionary history than where they live or what they eat. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why Great Plains rivers depend on wetlands as well as climate
item.description: When a prairie river carries more water in one year than another, the obvious place to look for an explanation is the sky. A year with more snow and rain should have more water in rivers. That was also how I initially thought about year-to-year changes in river flow. But while studying the Prairie Pothole Region, I learned that this is only part of the story. What happens after water reaches the ground can be just as important as how much falls from the sky. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Controlling the brain with light earns a physiology Nobel
item.description: The entire field of optogenetics traces back to light-seeking algae. Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: John Timmer

item.description: NASA astronaut and mission specialist of the agency’s Artemis II mission, Christina Koch, leads the fans in singing the Eagles Fight Song from the field at an NFL game between the Philadelphia Eagles and the Los Angeles Rams at Lincoln Financial Field on Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026, in Philadelphia. item.title: Why can't people regenerate limbs like salamanders?
item.description: Imagine losing an arm and simply growing a new one. This amazing ability of regeneration isn't just something from a superhero movie—it actually happens in real life for some animals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Pollen study reveals the hidden history of grasses
item.description: Scientists used machine learning and super-resolution microscopy to overcome a challenge that has stymied research into the natural history of grasses for decades. Their method allowed them to detect subtle differences among grass pollen grains and trace changes in grass diversity and the proportions of the two main photosynthetic types of grasses at one site over a period of 25,000 years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Lightsaber-like plasma antenna uses laser-ionized air to transmit radio waves
item.description: Researchers have demonstrated a technique that uses a laser to produce a plasma beam antenna capable of transmitting radio waves. The article, "Laser-Induced-Plasma-Filament Antenna Transmitting 30 MHz VHF," is published in the IEEE Journal of Microwaves. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: En los años 90, unos investigadores descubrieron unas algas que reaccionaban increíblemente rápido a la luz. Hoy son el Nobel de Medicina
item.description: En el día de hoy se ha dado el pistoletazo de salida que inicia una de las semanas en el mundo científico y cultural más importantes de todo el año, como son los premios Nobel. Y como es tradicional, ha dado inicio con la lectura del veredicto del jurado en la disciplina de medicina y fisiología , que este año ha concedido el Nobel a Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann y Georg Nagel. Hay razones. Detrás de un premio tan importante como un Nobel lógicamente debe haber unas razones de peso para concederlo, y en esta ocasión el hito que galardona es importante por todo lo que ha conllevado a… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: José A. Lizana

item.title: Lipid signals help cells seal the damage from bacterial attacks, researchers discover
item.description: Epithelial cells form the body's frontline barriers, helping keep microbes, toxins and other harmful substances out. Yet these protective cells are constantly exposed to threats, including microbial infections. Some bacteria produce pore-forming toxins that can oligomerize and act like microscopic drills, perforating the cell's plasma membrane. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Resource scarcity influences maternal brain activity and caregiving in rats
item.description: When mothers do not have the necessary resources to raise their children, this adversity causes substantial stress that can hinder caregiving and lead to postpartum depression. In a new study in JNeurosci, Millie Rincón-Cortés and colleagues from the University of Texas at Dallas used rats to explore how a lack of resources while raising pups alters neural activity. The researchers focused on a neuron population that is activated by interactions with pups and is linked to motivated behavior as well as maternal care. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Space radiation sparks: A biological cascade of cancer
item.description: Deep space travel comes with a huge potential downside—radiation exposure that can kill an astronaut either quickly or slowly over time if not managed correctly. But what exactly does that mean, and is there any way to handle it other than sticking more and more protective layers between the squishy biological systems inside a spacecraft and the radiative void of deep space? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tiny ancient black holes may live in a five-dimensional world
item.description: Primordial black holes (PBHs) don't exist as far as we know. But if they did, these hypothetical objects would have formed in the early universe rather than from dying stars, and they may even make up dark matter. That's not the end of the weirdness. Their formation could have been even stranger if it occurred in a universe with a dark dimension, which is another theoretical construct. It posits that our space includes a hidden extra spatial dimension. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Farmer-macaque conflict in Algeria poses a complicated conservation challenge
item.description: One of the hardest challenges in wildlife conservation arises when the habitat of a species in need of protection overlaps with land used by humans. Wolves and bears can kill livestock, elephants can damage homes and other property and wild boar can damage crops. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: X-rays and AI reveal how spacecraft heat shields burn in real time
item.description: Heat shields are one of the most important parts of any spacecraft that intends to enter an atmosphere. And the material they are made of is critical. Improving them has been a challenge, though, as researchers typically only get "before" and "after" pictures of a heat shield's job of helping a spacecraft land safely back on Earth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Flying rivers' above South America form drainage networks resembling those on land
item.description: Water does not flow only through rivers on the ground. Vast quantities of water also move through the atmosphere, carried by winds from oceans and land before eventually falling as precipitation hundreds or even thousands of kilometers away. These persistent pathways of atmospheric moisture are often referred to as "aerial rivers" or "flying rivers." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ofsted wields great power in school choices, research finds
item.description: Ofsted reports are an influential factor parents consider when choosing an elementary school, with families abandoning schools after poor reports, according to new research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Testing Aims at Supercooled Large Droplet Aviation Safety
item.description: NASA is leveraging its expertise and enhancing its test facilities to help address a rare but persistent aviation hazard: icing that occurs when aircraft encounter unusually large, very cold water droplets in clouds. The problem, known as “supercooled large droplet icing,” occurs when aircraft fly through clouds containing unusually large drops of water that are […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Dede Dinius

item.title: How rotting food in the kitchen and a whiff of vinegar led to a 'happy' agricultural accident
item.description: Rutgers scientists have identified natural repellents against an invasive blueberry pest, a discovery made accidentally when fruit flies invaded their laboratory. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study finds that to counter misinformation online, we need to copy its style
item.description: Imagine you're worried about vaccinating your baby. A message on Facebook tells you: "Protect the community and your kids by booking their vaccinations today." Another asks: "Do you know all the effects of childhood vaccinations on your babies?" Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Suspected Second-generation Planet Solves NASA Hubble Cold Case
item.description: New analysis of archival Hubble data points to the possibility of “dead” white dwarf stars hosting second-generation planetary systems. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: The phoenix planet: Astronomers find a world reborn from its star's ashes
item.description: Astronomers have discovered the first example of a second-generation planet orbiting a white dwarf, a world that appears to have formed from the remains of the dead star it now orbits. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: International study finds ethnic minorities have less trust in police
item.description: A new study led by an academic staff member from the University of Otago – Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka has analyzed trust between police and ethnic minorities in Aotearoa New Zealand and the United States, revealing meaningful similarities between Māori and Black Americans. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Extinct bovine species discovered in Siberia reveals lost relative of yaks
item.description: DNA analyses of ancient remains have revealed a previously unknown extinct bovine species that inhabited southern Siberia during and even before the last ice age. The extinct species was related to modern yaks but followed a separate evolutionary path for hundreds of thousands of years. The findings are published in Current Biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Decades of data reveal major ecological shift in northern Baltic Sea
item.description: For decades, scientists have regarded phosphorus as the main nutrient limiting biological production in the Gulf of Bothnia. Now, a new study led by researchers at Umeå University shows that a fundamental change is underway. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: We know how to end homelessness. We just won't pay for it
item.description: Japan has the lowest measured rate of homelessness of any wealthy nation. Finland is the only country in Europe that has driven homelessness down over decades rather than watched it climb. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers are tracking a Chinese AI ‘agent fleet’
item.description: Independent researchers discovered an agent swarm that seems to be running on Tencent's infrastructure and targeting Alibaba's map service, Amap. Fuente: TechCrunch.
item.dc:creator: Russell Brandom

item.title: Heat-induced nanoscale structures unlock electromechanical properties in ceramics
item.description: Scientists have developed a new way to make ceramic materials that can better withstand extreme heat and continue performing reliably in sensors and actuators. The approach creates tiny structures throughout the material that give it new electrical and mechanical properties. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Kauri dieback threatens more than trees—it could change how much carbon forests store
item.description: Kauri are among Aotearoa New Zealand's tallest and longest-lived trees—and their place in our cultural landscape looms equally large. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nobel medicine prize honours US and German scientists for optogenetics work
item.description: American Karl ⁠Deisseroth and Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on Monday for developing optogenetics, a technique that uses light to control individual nerve cells in the brain. Publicado también por: South China Morning Post. Fuente: Al Jazeera English.

item.title: Precision IVF tracks how mouse embryos switch on their genome
item.description: A new study from EMBL Rome shows how embryos precisely coordinate gene activity during early development. The research is published in the journal Science Advances. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tribal members saw pinyon-juniper woodlands declining, new study confirms
item.description: Pinyon pines and juniper trees spread across the mid-elevation slopes of the American West, including California's Eastern Sierra. These hardy, short-statured trees are one of the most widespread vegetation types on federal lands, covering more than 100 million acres (405,000 square kilometers) across 10 Western states. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Manganese-doped carbon nanodots could rival existing MRI contrast agents
item.description: Contrast agents are compounds routinely used in clinical analysis to enhance differentiation between tissues or to increase the visibility of structures or fluids within the body, thus facilitating medical diagnosis. A study led by researcher Lucia Cardo and Ikerbasque research professor and AXA chair Maurizio Prato (both at CIC biomaGUNE) confirms that manganese-doped carbon nanodots could be the next generation of contrast agents for magnetic resonance imaging. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists reveal what seven days of fasting does to the human body
item.description: Scientists found that prolonged fasting triggers major changes throughout the body, but many of the most interesting effects only appeared after about three days without food. The results suggest fasting may influence health in ways that go beyond weight loss and could eventually inspire treatments that mimic its effects. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: El "interruptor de luz" para neuronas por el que 3 científicos ganaron el Nobel de Medicina y que ayuda a descifrar los misterios del cerebro
item.description: Te explicamos qué es la optogenética, la disciplina por la que Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann y Georg Nagel ganaron el Nobel de Medicina. Fuente: BBC News Mundo.

item.title: Vagus Nerve Stimulation Could Help New Skills Stick
item.description: Stimulating the vagus nerve after practice helped mice develop stronger long-term motor learning, revealing a potentially important window when the brain is still locking in a new skill. The effect was linked to rhythmic changes in brain blood vessels, hinting that body-to-brain signals may help prepare the brain for lasting change. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Security, sacrifice or opportunity: Visions differ over effective climate action
item.description: Should the world move away sharply from fossil fuels, or manage a slower, more careful retreat? Fuente: UN News.

item.title: Espacio: la revolución de los cohetes democratiza el acceso a la órbita
item.description: Cohetes reutilizables, empresas privadas, universidades y nuevos actores nacionales han abaratado el acceso a la órbita, y se prevé que la economía espacial mundial alcance el billón de dólares en 2030. "Un mayor acceso al espacio conlleva una mayor responsabilidad", advierte Aarti Holla-Maini, directora de la UNOOSA, que reclama más cooperación internacional para gobernar un espacio cada vez más concurrido. Fuente: Noticias ONU.

item.title: Don't miss: Watch Saturn shine and Halley’s Comet debris streak across the sky
item.description: October skywatchers can see Saturn at opposition, catch meteors from Halley’s Comet during the Orionid peak, and watch the Moon sweep past the famous Pleiades star cluster. Moonlight may obscure some Orionids, but the best viewing should come before dawn after the Moon sets. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A new kind of magnetism could unlock faster, more efficient computers
item.description: Scientists have discovered evidence of altermagnetism in a thin, highly tunable material that could help electronics use electron spin instead of relying only on electrical charge. The unusual magnetic state may enable faster, more energy-efficient devices without the unwanted magnetic interference caused by conventional magnets. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists just found a way to fight lung cancer and muscle wasting at the same time
item.description: A new nanoparticle therapy reduced lung tumors in mice while also targeting cachexia, the severe muscle wasting that can accompany cancer. By delivering follistatin mRNA directly to tumors, the approach could eventually offer a way to fight both the disease and one of its most dangerous complications. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover a human brain gene that can jump through DNA
item.description: Scientists have discovered a human gene with a remarkable double life: it appears to play an important role in brain cells while still retaining the ability to jump around the genome. Called BC200, the gene evolved millions of years ago from a mobile piece of DNA known as a transposon, but unlike most genes that arose this way, it never lost its mobility. Researchers even found BC200 embedded inside a human poxvirus, suggesting it may have jumped from infected skin cells into the virus. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Cancer-fighting t cells burn out. Scientists may have found a fix
item.description: Cancer immunotherapy can lose its punch when tumor-fighting T cells become exhausted, but researchers may have found a way to keep them going longer. Scientists at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center identified a signaling molecule called MEK that can push T cells to burn through their energy while producing cancer-killing proteins. In animal and laboratory studies, blocking MEK helped the cells conserve energy, survive longer, and remain active even in the harsh environment around tumors. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Electrical technique could help identify signs of life in space
item.description: The truth is out there—but identifying signs of life in space involves an intense search for biosignatures within our solar system and beyond. However, developing sensitive yet compact technologies capable of detection has proven to be an out-of-this-world challenge. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Extreme heat putting pregnant women, newborns at risk: UN climate chief
item.description: Extreme heat is putting pregnant mothers and their newborns at increasing risk, United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell will warn on Monday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA spacecraft gains 3.5 km/s speed from Earth’s gravity assist without major engine burn
item.description: On September 28, 2026, Juice, the Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer, accomplished a successful gravity assist flyby of Earth. This maneuver was pivotal in adjusting the spacecraft's trajectory and significantly boosting its speed without the need for extensive engine thrust. Throughout its mission, Juice has strategically employed gravity assists, effectively conserving fuel. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Research into weight-loss drugs tipped for Nobel as award week opens
item.description: Research into hormones that regulate appetite is on everybody's lips for the Nobel medicine prize, to be announced on Monday when the 2026 Nobel season kicks off. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sunken Silk Road city reveals Central Asia's lost history
item.description: The sun had barely risen, but diving volunteer Elizaveta Bodrova was already raring to plunge into the cold waters of Lake Issyk-Kul, where the ruins of a once-thriving city have lain submerged for centuries. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: This mysterious hole on the Moon may open into a giant cave
item.description: NASA has selected the GIMLI project to investigate whether the Marius Hill Pit opens into a vast underground cave or lava tube. Using radar, seismic sensors, gravity measurements, and cameras, researchers will search beneath the lunar surface and estimate the size of any hidden void. Such caves could preserve clues to the Moon’s volcanic history and potentially provide protected shelters for future astronauts. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.description: A bright lens of anorthosite, a rock type prevalent on the lunar surface, is cradled within sheared rocks in the country’s south. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Modern forensics reveals human sacrifice in ancient Egypt's royal burials
item.description: Over 500 years before the building of the Great Pyramid in Egypt, First Dynasty kings were buried in a tomb surrounded by many burials of household officials and artisans—many of which seem to have taken place at the same time, a suspiciously high number of simultaneous deaths. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The “glue” holding your cells together has a surprising second job
item.description: Scientists have discovered that E-cadherin, a protein best known as the “glue” holding cells and tissues together, has a surprising second job: helping epithelial cells swallow nearby dead cells. Using live zebrafish and mouse embryos, researchers found that cells can dramatically reshape their lower surfaces to engulf cellular debris while keeping their upper surfaces stable, allowing protective barriers to remain sealed. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: DNA reveals the origin of rats found on Lord Howe Island after eradication
item.description: Black rats were believed to have been completely eliminated from Lord Howe Island, only for researchers to rediscover them in 2021. Through genetic analysis, they traced the rats back to the island’s prior population rather than any from the mainland of New South Wales. This finding sparked debates about how these rodents survived the eradication. Consequently, a swift initiative was launched to eradicate the newly returned rats. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Easing constipation: A 20-minute walk can get your gut moving almost immediately
item.description: Researchers found that just 20 minutes of comfortable walking can rapidly stimulate the gut. Within one to two minutes after exercise, bowel sounds became stronger, more frequent, and lasted longer, suggesting increased intestinal movement. The boost was brief, fading within a few minutes, but it may help explain why walking can provide relief from constipation. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Nanoneedle arrays map RNA in fresh tissue without sequencing or amplification
item.description: Recently, spatial omics has become a powerful tool, enabling researchers to see not only what molecules are present in a tissue, but also where they are located and how they are organized across cells, tissue structures and local microenvironments. This spatial context has deepened our understanding of cancer, neurobiology and immunology. Yet as the field advances, an important question remains: How many of these powerful technologies are ready for routine clinical use? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Informal businesses belong in entrepreneurial ecosystems, review argues
item.description: A systematic review of informal businesses published in the International Journal of Entrepreneurship and Small Business argues that they should be treated as part of the larger entrepreneurial ecosystem rather than as a peripheral feature of the economy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: If you've ever felt overwhelmed by menu options at a restaurant, cereal varieties at the grocery store or potential partners while scrolling through dating apps, you've experienced choice overload. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 3 million face masks could be used to build 1 km road, Australian study finds
item.description: Engineers at RMIT University have discovered a groundbreaking method to recycle single-use face masks by integrating them into road construction. By blending shredded masks with recycled concrete aggregate, the researchers aim to enhance road materials while tackling the problem of mask waste. Their findings suggest that approximately 3 million masks could be utilized in constructing a one-kilometre, two-lane road. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Gamma-ray search sets new limits on dark matter annihilation in the inner Milky Way
item.description: Dark matter could be a type of matter in the universe that does not emit, absorb or reflect detectable light and appears to interact very weakly with regular matter. Although physicists have observed gravitational effects attributed to dark matter, they have not yet been able to determine what it is made of. Fuente: Phys.org.
